title: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition) · Units 93–94
description: Advanced metaphorical concepts, figurative idioms, fixed phrases for success and setbacks, conversational reactions, confusion and emotional states.
sourceNotice: Prepared for personal study using the user-provided textbook as a source of vocabulary topics and targets. All definitions, Portuguese translations, teaching notes and examples are independently written; source exercises, extended passages and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Unit 93 teaching sections A–C, examples and exercises 93.1–93.4; Unit 94 teaching sections A–D and exercises 94.1–94.5; related answer-key entries. Literary quotations from the exercise are interpreted for coverage but not reproduced as cards.
audit.pronunciation: British English is the baseline. IPA appears only for isolated short entries where transcription is reasonably confident; longer idiomatic phrases have blank IPA rather than speculative connected-speech transcription.
audit.languagePolicy: English-only titles, metadata, notes, objectives, examples and sections; Brazilian Portuguese translations exclusively in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Read the complete teaching and exercise pages, inspected the source illustrations and checked relevant answer-key entries. Curated textbook targets and exercise-only idioms separately, wrote independent example sentences and usage notes, and checked semantic contrasts. Reopened the final JSON and validated schema parity, required fields, types, unique IDs and static word/sentence-audio target rules.
audit.limitations: No MP3 recordings are bundled. Actual VocabLab import, browser speech synthesis and speech recognition were not tested. Interpretations of extended literary metaphors remain outside the flashcard scope.

units.title: Unit 93 — Metaphor: seeing the light
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 192–193 (PDF pages 194–195).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Figurative language · metaphors, imagery and idioms
learningObjectives: Recognise literal and metaphorical meanings and explain the images behind common idioms.
Use body, sport and travel metaphors with natural grammar and prepositions.
Identify productive metaphorical concepts involving light, heat, water, time and business.
Interpret relevant exercise-only idioms without reproducing literary quotations.

sectionsChecked: Teaching sections and their contextual examples

items.example: Calling an office a battlefield is a metaphor for constant conflict.
items.note: A metaphor describes something indirectly by borrowing features from another domain.

items.example: She understood the instruction in its literal sense rather than as a joke.
items.note: Literal meaning contrasts with an abstract or figurative interpretation.

items.pt: selva urbana; cidade caótica e perigosa
items.example: The film portrays the capital as an urban jungle in which newcomers struggle to survive.
items.note: Figuratively compares a city with an environment seen as dangerous or difficult.

items.pt: iluminar a vida de alguém; trazer felicidade
items.example: Their adopted daughter has truly lit up their lives.
items.note: Figurative light represents joy, encouragement or renewed hope.

items.pt: estar atento e preparado; estar por dentro
items.example: The new supervisor is on the ball and notices problems before they escalate.
items.note: From sport: alert, well-informed and ready to act.

items.word: keep a tight rein on spending
items.example: The organisation must keep a tight rein on unnecessary expenditure.
items.note: From horse riding; keep strict control over somebody or something. Spending is a natural sample object.

items.word: in the heart of the city
items.pt: no coração da cidade; na região central
items.example: The conference venue is in the heart of the city, close to the main station.
items.note: Heart metaphorically means the central or most important part.

items.example: The fishing boats returned through the mouth of the river at dusk.
items.note: Mouth is the point where a river meets the sea or another body of water.

items.pt: dirigente; responsável máximo por uma organização
items.example: The head of the organisation presented the annual strategy to staff.
items.note: Head means the person with overall authority.

items.word: have an eye for a bargain
items.pt: ter faro para boas ofertas; saber encontrar pechinchas
items.example: Her grandfather has an eye for a bargain at antique markets.
items.note: Have an eye for means be skilled at noticing a particular quality or opportunity.

items.word: keep a close eye on progress
items.example: Engineers kept a close eye on the temperature during the endurance test.
items.note: Keep a close eye on something means monitor it carefully, often for safety or progress; progress is an example object.

items.example: The children are in safe hands with the experienced carers.
items.note: Implies that the person responsible is capable and trustworthy.

items.pt: andar de mãos dadas com; estar intimamente ligado a
items.example: Technological progress often goes hand in hand with new ethical questions.
items.note: Go hand in hand with something means develop together or be closely connected; typically followed by with.

items.example: As a rule of thumb, allow extra time for each verification cycle.
items.note: A useful approximate guideline, not a precise law or measurement.

items.example: She is a bright researcher with an instinct for finding patterns.
items.note: Figuratively associates intelligence with light; avoid interpreting it as physical brightness here.

items.example: The fictional detective pretends to be dim so that others underestimate him.
items.note: Informal, often disparaging when applied to intelligence.

items.example: After reviewing the evidence, the panel finally saw the light.
items.note: Understanding is imagined as illumination; can imply a change of opinion.

items.example: The audit cast light on why the equipment had repeatedly failed.
items.note: Make something easier to understand by supplying new information.

items.pt: oscilar entre entusiasmo e desinteresse; mudar constantemente de opinião
items.example: The investors kept blowing hot and cold about the proposed expansion.
items.note: Alternating between positive and negative attitudes.

items.example: His hotheaded response made the delicate negotiation harder.
items.note: Reacting from strong feelings before thinking carefully.

items.example: The character initially seems cold-hearted but gradually shows compassion.
items.note: Describes a perceived lack of empathy, not body temperature.

items.example: Even when the debate became heated, the chair managed to keep cool.
items.note: Staying calm under emotional pressure; often contrasted with hotheaded behaviour.

items.pt: sair em massa; sair em grande quantidade
items.example: Spectators flooded out of the stadium after the final whistle.
items.note: Water imagery for a large number of people moving quickly.

items.pt: sair aos poucos; sair em pequenos grupos
items.example: The delegates trickled out of the hall after the closing remarks.
items.note: Opposite image to flood out; a slow, sparse flow of people.

items.example: A steady stream of traffic passed the laboratory all morning.
items.note: Stream uses a water image for continuous movement of vehicles.

items.example: Stewards regulated the flow of people through the narrow exit.
items.note: Movement of a crowd is conceptualised as flowing liquid.

items.example: We spent considerable time checking the assumptions behind the model.
items.note: Time is treated metaphorically as a resource that can be spent.

items.example: Don't waste time polishing minor details before the core design works.
items.note: Implies that the time yields little value.

items.example: She invested time in learning a tool that would later improve productivity.
items.note: Time is spent now in the expectation of a future benefit.

items.example: The team's investment in documentation paid dividends during maintenance.
items.note: Originally financial; figuratively means produce worthwhile benefits.

items.example: Automating the routine checks saved the team several hours each week.
items.note: Time is conceptualised as something that can be saved like money.

items.example: Their marketing strategy focused on customers who value reliability.
items.note: The unit links business strategy to military planning.

items.example: The company changed its pricing tactics after testing customer responses.
items.note: Tactical actions are shorter-term methods supporting a larger strategy.

items.example: The publisher launched an advertising campaign aimed at international readers.
items.note: Launch and campaign borrow the imagery of organised operations.

items.example: The regional teams achieved their sales targets despite the downturn.
items.note: Target comes from aiming at a goal, as in sport or military language.

items.pt: estar no comando; assumir as rédeas
items.example: The deputy director will hold the reins while the director is away.
items.note: Horse-riding imagery for being in charge; closely related to keep a tight rein on.

items.pt: mudar as regras no meio do processo; alterar os critérios
items.example: The client moved the goalposts after the team had agreed on the specification.
items.note: From sport; change the criteria after work has begun, often unfairly.

items.pt: ideia mal elaborada; plano pouco amadurecido
items.example: The board rejected the half-baked idea because nobody had considered the costs.
items.note: Baking imagery: not sufficiently thought through or developed.

items.example: Families may need to tighten their belts during prolonged inflation.
items.note: Spending less because money is scarce; plural tighten our belts is common.

items.pt: considerar e aceitar; incorporar uma sugestão
items.example: The designers took the accessibility feedback on board before releasing the prototype.
items.note: Image of loading cargo onto a ship; absorb and act on information or feedback.

items.pt: dentro do cronograma; no caminho certo
items.example: The project is on track to meet its revised deadline.
items.note: Travel imagery for making the expected progress toward a goal.

items.example: Technicians worked around the clock to restore the service.
items.note: Means continuously, including overnight.

items.pt: aceitar pelo valor aparente; acreditar sem questionar
items.example: Reviewers should not take the manufacturer's performance claims at face value.
items.note: Accept an appearance or statement without checking for hidden complications.

items.example: The newly released records throw fresh light on the early investigation.
items.note: A variant of cast light on that emphasises new understanding.

units.title: Unit 94 — Idioms for everyday situations and feelings
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition); printed pages 194–195 (PDF pages 196–197).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Advanced (3rd Edition)
units.category: Idioms · success, setbacks, confusion and emotions
learningObjectives: Describe successful plans using precise fixed idioms.
React naturally to setbacks and unexpected difficulties in conversation.
Express happiness, suitability, frustration and sadness with correct fixed phrases.

sectionsChecked: Teaching sections and their contextual examples

items.example: The revised booking system worked like a dream throughout the pilot.
items.note: Used when a plan or process performs exceptionally well.

items.pt: funcionar como um relógio; transcorrer sem problemas
items.example: The conference ran like clockwork despite the complicated schedule.
items.note: Also go like clockwork; implies smooth, predictable operation.

items.example: The replacement server was up and running before the office opened.
items.note: Emphasises that a system or activity has started functioning as intended.

items.pt: começar a se encaixar; dar certo gradualmente
items.example: Once the funding was approved, the other parts of the programme began to fall into place.
items.note: Separate elements gradually form a coherent, workable whole.

items.example: Business began to look up after the company entered new markets.
items.note: Said of prospects or a situation improving.

items.example: The printers have stopped working as well? That's all we need.
items.note: Ironic reaction when a further problem worsens an existing situation.

items.word: that's the last thing I wanted to hear
items.pt: era a última coisa que eu queria ouvir
items.example: A further delay is the last thing I wanted to hear before the launch.
items.note: Reacts to disappointing news that confirms a fear.

items.pt: como um pesadelo; como se tudo estivesse dando errado
items.example: With one mistake following another, the trip felt like a bad dream.
items.note: Suggests a sequence of distressing events, not an actual dream.

items.pt: um verdadeiro pesadelo; uma situação terrível
items.example: Resolving the insurance dispute became a real nightmare.
items.note: Figurative and often informal; usually not referring to sleep.

items.example: Another form to complete? What a pain!
items.note: Informal response to inconvenience or trouble.

items.pt: deixar alguém totalmente sem reação; pegar de surpresa
items.example: The unexpected question threw the spokesperson completely.
items.note: Confuse or unsettle someone so that they cannot respond readily.

items.pt: uma completa bagunça; um caos organizacional
items.example: The registration process was a complete shambles, with long queues and missing forms.
items.note: Strongly negative British-English expression for a chaotic, badly organised situation.

items.pt: para mim é um mistério; não consigo entender
items.example: It's a mystery to me how that error escaped three reviews.
items.note: Used when the speaker cannot explain or understand something.

items.pt: ter um desencontro de informações; entender algo errado na comunicação
items.example: We got our wires crossed and reserved different rooms for the same meeting.
items.note: Informal idiom for miscommunication between people.

items.pt: não estou acompanhando o raciocínio; não entendi
items.example: I'm not with you on the last step of your explanation; could you clarify it?
items.note: Polite conversational way to signal difficulty understanding.

items.pt: você me perdeu nessa parte; não consegui acompanhar
items.example: You've lost me there; how does the second result follow from the first?
items.note: Conversational signal that the explanation has become hard to follow.

items.example: She felt on top of the world after receiving the scholarship.
items.note: Very happy or elated following good news.

items.example: He was on cloud nine when his first article was accepted.
items.note: The fixed expression uses nine, not other numbers.

items.example: The parents were over the moon with their daughter's progress.
items.note: Especially common in British English for intense happiness.

items.pt: no seu ambiente ideal; à vontade fazendo algo que domina
items.example: As soon as the discussion turned to robotics, she was in her element.
items.note: A person is in a setting or activity that suits their interests and abilities.

items.pt: ser feito para; ter perfil ideal para
items.example: With his patience and eye for detail, he seems made for quality assurance.
items.note: Be ideally suited for an activity or role; followed by a noun or -ing form depending on context.

items.word: fed up to the back teeth
items.pt: farto até não aguentar mais; de saco cheio
items.example: Residents are fed up to the back teeth with the constant construction noise.
items.note: Strong, informal British expression for extreme frustration; fixed preposition to.

items.example: After the unsuccessful application, she felt down in the dumps for a few days.
items.note: Informal idiom for being sad or low in spirits, not a diagnosis.

items.example: He looked rather down in the mouth after hearing the result.
items.note: Similar to down in the dumps; often describes how someone looks.

items.pt: a gota d'água; o limite da paciência
items.example: The final unexpected charge was the last straw, so they cancelled the contract.
items.note: A final problem that makes an already difficult situation intolerable.

items.example: I still can't get my head round the new licensing conditions.
items.note: Informal British expression for understanding something difficult; also get your head around.

items.example: She looked as miserable as sin after spending the day alone in the rain.
items.note: Informal emphatic simile for looking or feeling very unhappy.

items.pt: funcionar perfeitamente; dar certo como mágica
items.example: The small configuration change worked like a charm and removed the warning.
items.note: Positive idiom for a solution that works extremely well, often unexpectedly.

items.pt: flutuar de felicidade; estar nas nuvens
items.example: He was walking on air all week after his promotion.
items.note: Describes great happiness, not literally walking above the ground.
